6Chapter 6 · The problem worth solving

A Plan Others Can Believe

A strategy is only a sentence until other people can act on it. Anaya learns to promise results, not dates. She writes goals as numbers that can be measured. She maps who can say no. She also runs a meeting that pretends the project has already failed.

11 min read10 new words

Retells app chapter A6

In this chapter

  • build an outcome roadmap with a kill criterion
  • write an objective with key results that measure what changed for people, plus an input metric and a guardrail
  • map stakeholders by power and interest, and act on the dangerous corner
  • write a decision memo, run a pre-mortem and list dependencies

Anaya spent years on delivery work for a utility rollout. Her plans looked like railway timetables. Her first manager had taught her how. Features went down the side. Months went across the top. Each feature got a bar that began on one date and ended on another. She had made about a dozen of these. She could not remember one that had come true.

The dates were usually wrong. But that was not the main flaw. Each bar was a promise to build something. None was a promise that the thing would help. When the dates slipped, the plan became a list of broken promises. When a feature turned out not to matter, it became a list of broken promises about the wrong thing.

The founders agreed in principle to the privacy tool. Then Anaya started a new plan on a clean page, with a different shape. This chapter looks at that shape and the goals attached to it. We also meet the people who could stop it. And we see a meeting that tested the plan before it began.

If you have run delivery, you know many of the words below. Stakeholder, dependency and risk list are old friends. Read for what changes. In delivery you own the date. Here you own the result.

6.1The case: a plan with no dates

The strategy from the last chapter was still only a sentence. Think of a destination on a map. People still need directions. For engineers, compliance staff and founders to act on it, three things were needed. First, an order of work. Second, a way to tell if the work succeeded. Third, an account of who could get in the way.

The sections below take those three in turn. Then comes a fourth step. It is a meeting where colleagues were asked to suppose the project had already failed.

6.2The outcome roadmap

A roadmap is a plan of what a team will work on, and roughly when. It is like a family's plan for the week. Tonight's dinner is fixed. Next week's shopping is likely. A holiday someday is a wish. Anaya's roadmap has three columns and no calendar.

  • Now holds the work the team is doing. It is a firm promise.
  • Next holds what the team expects to do afterwards. It is likely, but it may change.
  • Later holds what the team is exploring. It is ordered by today's thinking. It is promised to nobody.

Each item is written as an outcome, a change in what people can do. It is not written as a feature. Under each item are a few lines of detail. Here is her entry for the first item.

The last line was new to her. A kill criterion is like a rule before a trek: "Turn back if we have not reached the bridge by noon." It is a condition, set in advance, that means the work stops.

It works for a human reason. After three weeks of effort, nobody can fairly judge if the work is going badly. Everyone has a reason to say it is going well. The rule is written at the start, before anyone is attached to the result. It describes failure in words that nobody has to argue about later.

Kill criteria matter even more when the work involves software that reads and writes text. You cannot know its accuracy in advance. You find it out by trying it. So a date promised before the first test is a guess dressed up as a promise.

Key idea

What changes when you own the outcome

Delivery and product ask for different promises. A delivery plan promises a date. The work is judged on whether it arrived. A product plan promises a result. The work is judged on whether something changed for the people who use it.

  • The date promised becomes the result promised.
  • The scope delivered becomes the number moved.
  • A risk escalated (passed up to a boss) becomes a kill criterion written down in advance.

6.3Goals and the numbers beneath them

Lakshmi's question was still on a sticky note on Anaya's desk. How would she know that the tool worked?

Companies answer this with objectives and key results, called OKR for short. Think of a report card. The objective says in words what you want. The key results are the marks beside it. They are three or four numbers that show you got there.

Key idea

Outcomes, not outputs

A key result measures an outcome, which is what changed for people. It does not measure an output, which is what was shipped. "Release the privacy tool" is an output. It can be done, and nothing may change. "Fewer conversations leave the chat with a personal detail in them" is an outcome.

Anaya wrote one objective and two key results. The objective was to make Sahaj's support chat safe to export. Export means to copy data out of a system. The first key result was about conversations leaving the chat with no unhidden personal detail. Their share would rise from 91 percent to 99 percent. The second key result was this. Support agents would report fewer than one chat in fifty where the tool had hidden something they needed.

Two other kinds of number sit beside key results.

An input metric is like counting your daily steps to lose weight. It is a number the team can move directly, and you expect it to move the result. For her it was the share of fixed-shape numbers the tool caught. You cannot order the result to change. But you can improve the input.

A guardrail metric is like the railing on a bridge. It is a number that must not get worse while the team chases the others. It stops you from winning in a way that does harm. Hers was the false-alarm rate. That is the share of hidden items that were not personal at all. A tool that blanked every number in every message would score perfectly on the first key result. And it would be useless. So she set the limit at three in a hundred.

One more difference was easy to lose once the work became technical. The tool would have its own score on its own test. That score measures the tool. The key results measure what happens to people.

A tool can do well on its own test, and still be ignored by agents who find it annoying. Or it can arrive too late to matter. Both kinds of number were needed. Each had to be labelled as one or the other.

6.4The people who can say no

Imran asked who would actually read the plan. Anaya did not know.

Think of the people at a wedding. The cook, the priest and the hall owner can each make it work or stop it. Anyone who can help or stop a project, or is affected by it, is a stakeholder. Stakeholders are not all equal. So Anaya drew a square with two lines. One line showed how much power a person had over the project. The other showed how much they cared about it. Then she placed names in it.

Beside each name she wrote what the person was measured on. That tells you how they will react. She also wrote what they could decide. Did they choose, advise, or have a veto (the right to say no and stop it)?

Lakshmi was in the wrong corner. She had real power. As far as Anaya could tell, she had little interest. That mix is the most dangerous. People in security, legal and compliance often hold a veto, while taking little part in the daily work.

They stay quiet until the day before launch. Then they say no. They are usually right to. On a government project, the same corner is usually held by audit (the people who check the books), finance or the security assessor.

The remedy was ordinary. Anaya visited Lakshmi every week and asked what she would need. That moved her into the second column.

6.5The decision memo

The founders would not read a plan. They would read the first paragraph of a memo, and maybe the second.

A decision memo is like a newspaper story. The first paragraph tells you everything. It is written so that a busy person can act after reading only the opening. The order is: the request, the reason, the cost, the biggest risk, and the other choices, including doing nothing. Here is Anaya's opening paragraph.

Worked example

Anaya's opening paragraph

I am asking for Imran for half his time for eight weeks, and about forty thousand rupees in cloud costs, to build a small tool that hides personal details in our support chat before they travel any further. In one week of chats, 37 of 400 conversations contained an identity number, a tax number, a bank account or an address, and nothing removes them from our logs, exports or the outside company's systems.

The biggest risk is that the tool misses things written in Hinglish. We will test it on real examples before it touches a live chat, and we will stop if agents turn it off in more than two of ten chats.

In four sentences, it states the ask, the proof, the main risk and the stopping rule.

6.6Supposing it has failed

Before the founders' meeting, Anaya held a gathering. Imran had dreaded it. Farah had looked forward to it. Everyone was to pretend it was six months later and the project had failed. Then each person wrote down, alone and without talking, why it failed.

This is a pre-mortem. It is like tasting the dish in your head and finding it burnt before you cook. It works for a simple reason. People will name risks in a pretend failure that they would not raise against a plan they are expected to back.

Farah wrote that agents had switched the tool off. It had hidden a customer's callback number in the middle of a talk. Nobody had told agents how to get it back. Lakshmi wrote that it had missed an address written in Hinglish. A screenshot had gone out in an export. A regulator had asked how that was possible. A regulator is the official body that checks that firms follow the law.

Imran wrote that it had added a second to every reply. Customers had complained that the chatbot felt slow. Anaya wrote that the file of test examples had never been kept up to date. So nobody could tell if the fourth version was better than the third.

Anaya turned all of this into a risk list.

Beside it she kept a shorter list of things she needed from other people. A dependency is like waiting for the plumber before you can paint the wall. It is anything the project needs from outside the team. It may be someone else's work, a supplier's help, access to data, or an approval. Dependencies are where plans slip, because nobody on the team controls them.

Hers were three. She needed read access to the chat system. She needed Lakshmi's sign-off (her written yes) before anything went live. And she needed a promise from the outside company that its software would not change how it accepted text. The first she could have by Friday. She was less sure of the third.

6.7The outcome

The founders spent eleven minutes on the memo. They asked how long it would take, how much it would cost, and whether Lakshmi had agreed. Anaya answered the third question first.

The decision went into the log she had begun on the first night. She added a new line beneath it. She would change her mind if Imran's half-time could not be spared beyond week three.

Think of a doctor who tells you the risks before the operation. You trust that doctor more, not less. A plan that others can believe does not sound the most confident. It has already told them how it might fail.

Chapter summary

A roadmap that promises results in Now, Next and Later columns breaks less often than one that promises features on dates. A kill criterion written at the start makes stopping easier.

  • An objective states the goal in words, and key results measure what changed for people. An input metric is a number the team can move directly. A guardrail metric must not get worse. A tool's own test score is a different thing from a key result.
  • Stakeholders differ in power and interest. A person with power and no interest is the one most likely to stop a project late.
  • A decision memo opens with the request, the proof, the main risk and the stopping rule.
  • A pre-mortem asks everyone to suppose the failure first. Its output is a risk list with owners. Dependencies, which the team does not control, are listed separately.

Next, Anaya writes the whole thing down so that the engineers can build from it.

Key terms

Plain meanings, in the order you meet them.

roadmap
like a family's plan for the week: tonight is fixed, next week is likely, someday is a wish; it shows what a team will work on and roughly when, in three columns, Now, Next and Later, with results promised instead of dates
kill criterion
like a trek rule, "turn back if we have not reached the bridge by noon"; a condition, written in advance, that means you stop the work
OKR
like a report card goal with marks beside it: objectives and key results, a goal in words with a few numbers that show you reached it
key result
like the marks that show you passed; one of the three or four numbers under a goal. It measures what changed for people, not what you shipped
input metric
like counting your daily steps to lose weight; a number the team can change directly, which you expect to move the result
guardrail metric
like the railing on a bridge; a number that must not get worse while you chase the key results
stakeholder
like the people at a wedding who can make it work or stop it, such as the cook and the hall owner; anyone who can help or stop a project, or is affected by it
decision memo
like a newspaper story whose first paragraph tells you everything; a short note a busy person can act on after reading its opening
pre-mortem
like tasting the dish in your head and finding it burnt before you cook; a meeting where everyone supposes the project has failed and writes down why
dependency
like waiting for the plumber before you can paint the wall; anything you need from outside your own team to finish
